title: coNP certificates for three-manifold homeomorphism
formal: Does nonhomeomorphism of connected compact triangulated 3-manifolds have polynomially bounded certificates verifiable in polynomial time? Allow boundary and nonorientable manifolds. Precisely, do there exist a polynomial \(p\) and a uniform deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(W\) such that for every promised pair \((T,U)\in\mathcal D\) with total input length \(N\), \[\neg H(T,U)\iff\exists w\in\{0,1\}^{\leq p(N)}\;W(T,U,w)=1?\] This is the coNP-certificate question for the promised homeomorphism problem.
why: The question asks whether topological difference always has efficiently checkable finite evidence. Its reduction from graph isomorphism ties the difficulty of distinguishing 3-manifolds to a central unresolved certificate problem in complexity theory.
status_note: The general coNP question is explicitly open in the 2024 report. The bounded search through 14 September 2026 found no general result meeting these unconditional quantifiers. Special Seifert naming certificates do not establish the full target.

progress.text: Lackenby proves the graph-isomorphism reduction to closed 3-manifold homeomorphism.
Schleimer poses the coNP question and discusses its connection to graph isomorphism.
Jackson proves two-sided certificates for a Seifert naming problem with boundary.

importance.reason: A broad certificate question for distinguishing topological types, with a consequential implication for graph nonisomorphism via the known many-one reduction.

sentences: The homeomorphism problem asks whether two triangulations represent the same three-dimensional space.
This card asks for short certificates precisely when those spaces are not homeomorphic.
Every nonhomeomorphic pair must have verifiable evidence, including pairs that agree on familiar invariants.
A general positive result would imply polynomial certificates for graph nonisomorphism through a known reduction.
It would clarify whether topological distinction has a uniformly efficient theory of verification.

definitions: A triangulation consists of \(t\geq1\) labelled copies of \(\Delta^3=\{x\in\mathbb R^4:x_i\geq0,\ \sum_{i=0}^3x_i=1\}\), with some triangular faces paired by affine bijections specified by permutations of their three vertices. Each face is unpaired or paired with one other face; a pairing to the identical face slot is forbidden, pairings are reciprocal, and different faces of the same tetrahedron may be paired. The realization \(|T|\) is the disjoint union of the tetrahedra modulo the stated identifications, with the quotient topology. The input promise is that each realization is a nonempty connected compact 3-manifold, possibly with boundary: every point has a neighborhood homeomorphic to an open subset of \(\mathbb R^3\) or of \(\mathbb R^2\times[0,\infty)\). Orientability is not promised and no orientation, boundary marking or distinguished submanifold is supplied. Homeomorphism means a continuous bijection with continuous inverse, with no orientation-preserving or boundary-label requirement. In dimension three this agrees with equivalence of PL triangulations; combinatorial isomorphism of the supplied tetrahedron lists is not required. For a concrete binary encoding, write \(t\) in unary followed by the \(4t\) face slots in label order, each recording an unpaired flag or a partner tetrahedron index, a two-bit face index and one of the six vertex permutations; tetrahedron indices use \(\lceil\log_2(t+1)\rceil\) bits. The two encodings are concatenated and their total bit length is \(N\). Let \(\mathcal D\) be the promised domain of such pairs and \(H(T,U)\) the assertion \(|T|\cong|U|\). Algorithms and verifiers are uniform deterministic multitape Turing machines with bit-operation cost, no advice, oracles or randomness. The certificate statements concern this promised domain: verifiers must halt in their polynomial time bound on all bit strings, but acceptance outside \(\mathcal D\) has no specified topological meaning.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that such \(p,W\) exist, or that none exist. A positive answer needs a short accepted witness for every nonhomeomorphic promised pair and rejection of every candidate witness for every homeomorphic promised pair. Verification time must be polynomial in \(N+|w|\) on every binary input. A particular invariant that distinguishes only some pairs is insufficient. A negative answer must rule out all polynomial certificate systems, rather than showing the inadequacy of one invariant or representation. Conditional upper bounds qualify only if the additional hypothesis is also proved.

context_blocks.text: Schleimer states this as Question 4, separately from NP membership and NP-hardness. Its quantifiers run over nonhomeomorphic pairs; changing the sign of the target changes which instances need certificates.

Different triangulations can share many familiar invariants without being homeomorphic. The card does not prescribe an invariant: an accepted certificate system may use any finite evidence, but it must be complete for every pair in the full domain.

Lackenby gives a polynomial-time many-one reduction from graph isomorphism to closed 3-manifold homeomorphism. Consequently a coNP certificate system for the domain here would also provide polynomial certificates for graph nonisomorphism. The implication runs from a manifold upper bound to a graph upper bound.

Jackson’s naming theorem provides both NP and coNP certificates within the compact orientable Seifert setting with nonempty boundary. These two-sided certificates apply to the specified naming problem, not arbitrary pairs of triangulated 3-manifolds.

A decidability theorem guarantees that a search eventually terminates. It does not bound the size of evidence for a negative answer by a polynomial. Similarly, an NP system for homeomorphic pairs supplies no general witness for the opposite answer.

If homeomorphism were both NP-hard under the valid-output reductions defined in the related hardness card and in coNP, then \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}\). This is a logical consequence of the two prospective results, not a proof that either is false.
